'''''Myoporum insulare''''', commonly known as '''common boobialla''', '''native juniper''',<ref name="SA" /> is a species of flowering plant in the figwort family [[Scrophulariaceae]] and is [[Endemism|endemic]] to coastal areas of Australia. It is a shrub or small tree which grows on dunes and coastal cliffs, is very salt tolerant and widely used in horticulture.[[File:Myoporum insulare IMG 20180202 141456 2 (25174324717).jpg|thumb|225px|''Myoporum insulare'' fruit]]
[[File:Myoporum insulare R.Br. (AM AK299064-1).jpg|thumb|225px|Fruit and flowers]]

==Description==
Boobialla varies in form from a prostrate shrub to a small, erect tree growing to a height of {{cvt|6|m}}. It has thick, smooth green leaves which are {{cvt|30–90|mm}} long and {{cvt|7–22|mm}} wide with edges that are either untoothed or toothed toward the apex. The leaves are egg-shaped and the upper and lower surfaces are the same dull green colour.<ref name=Chinnock>{{cite book|last1=Chinnock|first1=Robert J.|title=Eremophila and allied genera: a monograph of the plant family Myoporaceae|date=2007|publisher=Rosenberg|location=Dural, NSW|isbn=978-1-877058-16-5|pages=108–110|edition=1st}}</ref><ref name=Costermans>{{cite book|author=Costermans, L.| title=Native Trees and Shrubs of South-eastern Australia |publisher=Rigby|location=Australia | year=1981 | isbn=0-7270-1403-X}}</ref><ref name=ANBG>{{cite web|last1=Marron|first1=Michele|title=Myoporum insulare|url=https://www.anbg.gov.au/gnp/interns-2010/myoporum-insulare.html|publisher=Australian National Botanic Garden|access-date=23 November 2015}}</ref>

White flowers with purple spots appear in the leaf axils in clusters of three to eight and are {{cvt|6–8|mm}} in diameter. There are five [[wikt:glabrous|glabrous]], smooth [[sepal]]s and the tube formed by the [[petal]]s is {{cvt|2.3–3.6|mm}} long with the lobes of the tube about the same length. The four [[stamen]]s usually extend slightly beyond the tube. Peak flowering times are July to February in Western Australia and October to December in south-eastern Australia. Flowering is followed by the fruit which is a smooth, rounded purple to black [[drupe]] {{cvt|4.5–9|mm}} in diameter.<ref name="Chinnock"/><ref name="Costermans"/><ref name="ANBG" /><ref name=NSW>{{cite web|last1=Chinnock|first1=Robert|title=Myoporum insulare|url=http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Myoporum~insulare|publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney, Plantnet|access-date=23 November 2015}}</ref>

==Taxonomy and naming==
''Myoporum insulare'' was first formally described by botanist [[Robert Brown (botanist, born 1773)|Robert Brown]] in ''[[Prodromus Florae Novae Hollandiae]]'' in 1810.<ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Myoporum insulare''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/509451|publisher=APNI|access-date=17 November 2020}}</ref><ref name=Brown>{{cite book|last1=Brown|first1=Robert|title=Prodromus Florae Novae Hollandiae|date=1810|volume=1 |publisher=Typis R Taylor, veneunt apud J. Johnson|location=London|page=516|url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/29583#page/384/mode/1up|access-date=23 November 2015}}</ref> The [[Botanical name|specific epithet]] ''[[wikt:insularis|insulare]]'' is a [[Latin]] word meaning "from an island".<ref name="RWB">{{cite book|last1=Brown|first1=Roland Wilbur|title=The Composition of Scientific Words|date=1956|publisher=Smithsonian Institution Press|location=Washington, D.C.|page=444}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
''Myoporum insulare'' occurs in coastal areas of [[New South Wales]], [[Victoria (state)|Victoria]], [[South Australia]], [[Western Australia]] and [[Tasmania]].<ref name="Chinnock" /> In New South Wales it occurs from [[Eden, New South Wales|Eden]] southward, although an isolated occurrence was recorded much further north on [[Brush Island]].<ref name="NSW" /> It is also found on [[Lord Howe Island]].<ref name=NSW/><ref name=DECC>{{cite web|title=Appendices Lord Howe Island Biodiversity Management Plan  |url=https://www.environment.gov.au/system/files/resources/e30dcdd3-e6d5-43e2-bc33-7fdb6dd9061e/files/lord-howe-island-appendices.pdf|publisher=Department of Environment and Climate Change (NSW)|access-date=23 November 2015}}</ref> In Victoria it is found in coastal areas but also inland in the west of that state.<ref name=Victoria>{{cite web|title=Common boobialla|url=http://vro.agriculture.vic.gov.au/dpi/vro/vrosite.nsf/pages/water_sss_common_boobialla|publisher=Victorian Resources Online|access-date=23 November 2015}}</ref> Boobialla is common along the coast of South Australia<ref name=SA>{{cite web | url =http://www.flora.sa.gov.au/cgi-bin/speciesfacts_display.cgi?form=speciesfacts&name=Myoporum_insulare | title =''Myoporum insulare'' | work = Electronic Flora of South Australia Fact Sheet | publisher = State Herbarium of South Australia|access-date=17 November 2020}}</ref> and in Western Australia it occurs south from [[Shark Bay]] to the South Australian border.<ref name=FloraBase>{{FloraBase|name=''Myoporum insulare'' |id= 7291|accessdate=2008-05-29}}</ref> It grows in sandy soils, often between rocks or near sandstone.<ref name="NSW" /><ref name="FloraBase" /> ''Myoporum insulare'' is invasive in several African countries and in the western coastal areas of the US. Invasive populations may include some other species of this genus. In South Africa this species is known as manatoka.<ref>Glen, Hugh & Van Wyk, Braam (2016) Guide to trees introduced into Southern Africa. pp230-231. Struik Nature, Cape Town</ref>

==Uses==
===Horticulture===
''Myoporum insulare'' may be used as a fast-growing [[hedge (barrier)|hedge]] or [[windbreak]] species which withstands coastal winds and drought.<ref>{{cite book|author=Cochrane, G.R., Fuhrer, B.A., Rotherdam, E.M., Simmons, J.& M. and Willis, J.H.| title=Flowers and Plants of Victoria and Tasmania |publisher=A.H. & A.W. Reed| year=1980 | isbn=0-589-50256-5}}</ref> It is hardy in well-drained positions and is easily propagated from cuttings.<ref name=Wrigley>{{cite book|last1=Wrigley|first1=John W.|last2=Fagg|first2=Murray|title=Australian native plants: a manual for their propagation, cultivation and use in landscaping|date=1983|publisher=Collins|location=Sydney|isbn=0-00-216575-9|pages=271–272|edition=2nd}}</ref> It is also used as [[rootstock]] for propagating many ''[[Eremophila (plant)|Eremophila]]'' species.<ref name="Boschen">{{cite book|last1=Boschen|first1=Norma|last2=Goods|first2=Maree|last3=Wait|first3=Russell|title=Australia's eremophilas: changing gardens for a changing climate|date=2008|publisher=Bloomings Books|location=Melbourne|isbn=978-1-876473-65-5|pages=23–24}}</ref>

===Bush tucker===
The purple fruit is edible,<ref name=coast>Ellis, M. & Norden, L. 2015. A Field Guide to Coastal Saltmarsh Plants in Victoria, South Gippsland Conservation Society, Inverloch. {{ISBN|9780959205008}}</ref> and  is good for making jams and jellies.<ref name=jams>{{cite web|url=https://tuckerbush.com.au/boobialla-myoporum-insulare-prostrate/ |title=Tucker Bush: Boobialla|access-date=31 May 2018}}</ref>
